intent: Test whether a larger drive wheel (radius 0.040 m, up from 0.035 m) raises average speed enough to finish the oval and s-bend in under 3 s. Sensor geometry, track width, mass and body are identical to Iteration 2, so the wheel radius is the only variable changed. Expected result: higher oval finish rate and lower completion_time than Iteration 2 (1.80 s), with off-track exits as the main risk.
learning: Hypotheses: (1) Radius 0.040 m raises the oval finish rate above 65% and cuts completion_time below 1.8 s, which would show the finish limit is speed, not sensing. (2) If off_track exits rise on the oval while max_error stays near 0.06 m, the speed gain is outrunning steering, so the next step is a wider wheel_track or lower mass rather than more speed. (3) If steering_oscillation stays near 0.28 and the finish rate does not move, the limit is controller tuning and the geometry is not the bottleneck. Only the 5-sensor, y=0.07 m, 16 mm layout is kept because the 7-sensor, y=0.08 m layout raised oscillation and lowered the oval finish rate.
rationale:
Evidence from the race data: Iteration 2 (5 sensors at y=0.07 m, 16 mm footprint, track 0.10 m, wheel radius 0.035 m, mass 0.6 kg) is still the best design at 329 points. Its oval finish rate was 65%, and its oval progress was 0.94. Iteration 3 moved the sensors to y=0.08 m and widened the array to 7 sensors. That raised s-bend progress from 0.45 to 0.48 but cut the oval finish rate to 35%, nearly doubled steering oscillation on the oval (0.28 to 0.36), and lowered the score to 272. Extra look-ahead and extra spread therefore did not pay off as a package, and the 7-sensor, y=0.08 m geometry looks like overshoot.

The oval failures are mostly off-track exits (7 of 20 in Iteration 2), while the oval mean finish time of about 1.80 s leaves about 1.2 s of margin under the 3.0 s limit. The completion term is worth 500 points, so a faster platform is the cheapest route to more finished runs on the held-back tracks. Wheel radius sets ground speed for a given wheel rotation rate, so raising it from 0.035 to 0.040 m should lift average speed by about 14% without touching the controller. The sensor layout is kept at the Iteration 2 values so this race isolates the drivetrain change. I expect oval completion to rise if the robot is speed-limited, but the risk is more off-track exits in bends, which is what I will look for in the telemetry.
